ch01.note: Tianbao (742–756) was the third and last reign-era of Emperor Xuanzong. From 744 its years were styled zai (载) rather than the usual nian (年), an archaizing usage the court adopted for the era; so the source’s 天宝三载 is ‘the third year of Tianbao,’ that is 744 CE. The fourteenth of the first lunar month falls in early spring.

ch01.anchor: the hour of the Snake, second half
ch01.note: The traditional day ran in twelve shichen, each equal to two modern hours and named for the twelve earthly branches and their zodiac animals. Each shichen divided into a first half (chu, 初) and a second half (zheng, 正); the Snake’s second half (si zheng, 巳正) centers on 10 a.m. The novel’s twenty-four chapters are the twenty-four half-shichen of one day, and each chapter is named for the hour it covers.

The Lantern Festival (Shangyuan, 上元) falls on the fifteenth night of the first lunar month; the chapter opens on its eve, the fourteenth. For its nights the capital’s strict curfew was suspended and the wards were hung with lanterns—the one season when Chang’an’s people could move freely after dark, and so the natural cover for the plot the Bureau fears.

The Sogdians were the Iranian merchant people of Central Asia who dominated Silk Road trade. Kang (康) was their city-state of Samarkand, chief among the ‘Nine Surnames of Zhaowu’ whose emigrants to China took surnames from their home cities—Cao, Kang, An, Shi, and the rest. The surname Cao thus marks the traveler, by his cover at least, as one of them.

A guosuo (过所) was the official permit required to move goods and persons through the empire’s checkpoints. It recorded the bearer, his party, and his cargo, and had to be inspected and sealed at every barrier along the road; to forge or misuse one was a grave offense.

ch01.anchor: a gold fish-pouch at his waist
ch01.note: Officials of the fifth rank and above wore a fish-shaped tally in a pouch at the belt as a badge of rank—gold for the third rank and up, silver below. The elder’s gold pouch marks a senior man; the young deputy’s silver one, as the narration later notes, is a grant from the emperor above his own sixth rank, a visible token of special favor.

The fly-whisk (fuchen, 拂尘) is a Daoist ritual implement; in the hand of an administrative officer it is incongruous, and it marks the young official’s Daoist bent. The historical Li Bi was famous for his Daoism and for repeatedly withdrawing to the mountains to practice it.

ch01.anchor: from the hand of Yan Zhenqing
ch01.note: Yan Zhenqing (709–785) was one of the supreme masters of Chinese calligraphy, his regular script celebrated for its full, upright strength. A real historical figure of the age; that the new Bureau’s name-board should be in his hand marks both its standing and its recent founding.

Özmiş Qaghan (r. 742–744) was the last ruler of the Second Turkic Khaganate. Historically a coalition of the Basmyl, Uyghurs, and Karluks broke his power and killed him in 744—the very year in which the novel is set—and his head was sent to the Tang court. The book’s frontier backdrop is thus genuine history; the account here is corroborated by the Tang annals.

The anecdote is drawn from the historical Li Bi’s biography: brought before Xuanzong as a boy prodigy, he capped the minister Zhang Yue’s verse on the chessboard and was rewarded with a place in the heir apparent’s study. Recorded in the Tang histories; corroborated. Li Bi (722–789) went on to serve four emperors as one of the dynasty’s most celebrated statesmen.

Zimei (子美) was the courtesy name of the poet Du Fu (712–770), who was living in and around Chang’an in just these years. The drunkard, taking the fleeing Cao Poyan for a friend, hails him by that name—a quiet authorial wink that the English can only footnote. Corroborated: Du Fu’s zi was indeed Zimei.

‘The Sage’ (shengren, 圣人) was a Tang court term of address for the reigning emperor, here Xuanzong (r. 712–756). The elder’s guarded phrase a moment later—‘that person,’ with a nod toward the palace—means the same man.

The Jing’an Bureau (Jing’an si, 靖安司) is the novel’s invention; no such standing security office existed in Tang Chang’an. The narrative supplies its own etymology—jing (靖) ‘to quell disorder,’ an (安) ‘peace’—and hands it a brief that the historical capital in fact divided among the Jinwu Guard, the Censorate, and the county constabularies. Its watchtower network and sand-table command room are likewise imaginative extrapolations from real Tang institutions.

ch01.anchor: a tall pavilion of black-lacquered timber
ch01.note: Watchtowers (wanglou, 望楼) did stand in the wards of Tang Chang’an as lookout posts against fire and theft. The novel’s semaphore network—flags by day, lanterns by night, relaying a message clear across the city in minutes—is an extrapolation from the frontier beacon-fire system (fengsui, 烽燧), as the text itself later observes.

The buliang-ren (不良人, literally ‘men of ill repute’) were the plainclothes thief-catchers and informers of the Tang capital, working the wards under a buliang chief (不良帅) who served as deputy to the constable-magistrate. The unflattering name is genuine; such runners were often reformed criminals set to catch their own kind. Zhang Xiaojing’s nine years as buliang chief of Wannian County make him exactly the underworld-wise operator the Bureau lacks.

The West Market (Xishi, 西市) was one of Chang’an’s two great government-licensed markets—the other being the East Market—a walled quarter of some two hundred trades that formed the eastern terminus of the Silk Road and the hub of the capital’s foreign commerce. It kept fixed hours announced by drum and was policed by a market office (市署); the throng of Sogdian, Persian, and other foreign merchants described here is historical.

ch01.anchor: a hundred and eight wards in all
ch01.note: Chang’an was laid out as a walled grid of enclosed residential wards (fang, 坊); ‘a hundred and eight’ is the traditional count. A night curfew (xiaojin, 宵禁) locked the ward gates at dusk and forbade movement on the main avenues until dawn, enforced by the Jinwu Guard—and was lifted only for the few nights around the Lantern Festival, which is what allows the novel’s plot to unfold across a single open night.

Sun Simiao (孙思邈, traditionally 581–682) was the great Tang physician and alchemist, author of the Beiji qianjin yaofang (‘Essential Prescriptions Worth a Thousand in Gold’) and revered after his death as the Medicine King (Yaowang, 药王). The Bureau’s taking over his former residence is the novel’s touch; he returns in Chapter Twenty-Four.

Mingguang (‘bright-light’) armor (明光铠) was the Tang heavy cuirass named for the large burnished metal discs at breast and back that flashed in the sun; it was the parade-and-battle armor of elite guardsmen. Its weight is what drags Cui Qi under the ice here.

ch01.anchor: The Lone Willow was the West Market
ch01.note: The Lone Willow (Duliushu, 独柳树) was a real execution ground—a solitary willow in the West Market where condemned criminals were beheaded, and a spot the superstitious shunned. The Tang carried out public executions in the markets, the assembled crowd serving as witness.

ch01.anchor: level as the Vermilion Bird Avenue
ch01.note: The Vermilion Bird Avenue (Zhuque dajie, 朱雀大街) was Chang’an’s central north–south axis, running from the palace city to the southern wall and dividing the capital into its two administrative counties—Chang’an to the west, Wannian to the east. Roughly 150 paces (about 150 metres) wide, it was the grandest thoroughfare in the medieval world; the Vermilion Bird (Zhuque) is the mythic red beast of the south.

Qujiang Pool (曲江池), in Chang’an’s southeast corner, was the capital’s great scenic lake-and-garden district, half within the walls and half without. Its shores held the imperial Furong (Lotus) Garden and were the setting for spring outings and for the banquet the court gave newly passed examination graduates. It recurs through the novel as both pleasure-ground and escape route.

ch01.anchor: Wang Zhongsi, Military Commissioner of Shuofang
ch01.note: Wang Zhongsi (王忠嗣, 705–749) was one of the great Tang frontier generals, at his height military commissioner of several border commands at once and the architect of the campaign breaking the Türk khaganate. Reared in the palace after his father died in battle, he was close to the heir apparent—which made him a target for Li Linfu, who engineered his ruin in 749. The abduction of his daughter here strikes at the linchpin of the whole Türk war.

ch02.note: He Zhizhang (659–744) was a celebrated Tang poet and official who served as Director of the Palace Library (Taichangqing / Secretary-General of the Imperial Clan Court, then Mishujian). A friend of Li Bai, he was famous for his poetry, his love of wine, and his nickname ‘the Drunken Sage of the Four Wisdoms.’ He retired to become a Daoist priest in 744, the very year the novel is set, and died shortly after. That the novel makes him the Jing’an Bureau’s nominal head is an invention—but his post as jian (Director) and his presence in Chang’an in early 744 are historical. Corroborated: biography in the Old Book of Tang and New Book of Tang.

Suluk (Çor) Khagan (r. 716–738) was the ruler of the Türgesh, a Western Turkic tribal confederation based in the Chu and Ili river valleys. He was a formidable adversary of both the Tang and the Umayyad Caliphate. The siege of Balhuan (拨换城, near modern Aksu in Xinjiang) is recorded in the Tang histories under the year 735 (Kaiyuan 23). The historical Gai Jiayun served as Protector-General of Beiting and did relieve the siege, though the novel embellishes the details. Suluk was assassinated by his own general Baga Tarkhan in 738. Corroborated: Zizhi Tongjian, juan 214; P. B. Golden, An Introduction to the History of the Turkic Peoples.

Cen Shen (岑参, c. 715–770) was one of the great Tang frontier poets, celebrated for his vivid depictions of the Western Regions. He was indeed from a family registered in Xianzhou (modern Nanyang, Henan). In 744 he would have been about twenty-nine, a young man not yet famous—his horse-and-poems cameo here is an authorial wink much like the Du Fu appearance in Chapter One. His first-person indignation at the burning of his verse is a charming irony, since the poems that survive made him immortal. Corroborated: standard biographical sources; see S. Owen, The Great Age of Chinese Poetry: The High T’ang.

Yama (Yanluo, 阎罗) is the king of the underworld and judge of the dead in Buddhist belief; to call a man a Yama is to name him a bringer of death. Zhang Xiaojing’s Wannian street-name, the ‘Five-Faced Yama’ (五尊阎罗), stacks five such demon-kings into one—the text glosses the five faces as vicious, venomous, ruthless, stubborn, and pitiless.

ch02.anchor: Zoroastrianism in Chang’an maintained no full monastery
ch02.note: Zoroastrianism (Xianjiao, 祆教)—the ancient Iranian religion of Ahura Mazda, centred on the veneration of a sacred fire—travelled the Silk Road into China and kept fire-temples in Tang Chang’an for its Sogdian and Persian community, licensed by the state under an appointed sabao (see Chapter Three). As the text notes, it did not seek Chinese converts. The camel-and-flame carvings and cinnabar ‘flame’ tiles here are the novel’s evocation of its architecture.

Hongfu, ‘Red Whisk’ or Lady Red Sleeve (红拂), is the heroine of the Tang tale The Curly-Bearded Hero (Qiuran ke zhuan, 虬髯客传): a great minister’s serving-girl who, smitten at first sight, slips away by night to elope with the then-penniless Li Jing, later Duke Li of Wei. Li Bi is teasing Tanqi not to run off with Zhang Xiaojing the same way.

ch02.anchor: It is better to employ the guilty than the meritorious
ch02.note: The maxim shi gong buru shi guo (使功不如使过, ‘better to employ a man who has erred than one who has earned merit’) holds that a person under a cloud will serve the harder to redeem himself. Tang tradition puts it in the mouth of Emperor Taizong when he spared and advanced the general Li Jing—the future Duke Li of Wei—whom others had urged him to punish. Li Bi cites it to justify staking everything on a condemned man.

ch02.anchor: Empress Wu Zetian had once taken the veil there
ch02.note: Wu Zetian (武则天, 624–705) began as a concubine of Taizong, became empress to his son Gaozong, and at last declared herself sovereign in her own right (r. 690–705)—the only woman ever to reign as emperor of China. On Taizong’s death she was sent, as custom required, to take the tonsure as a nun before Gaozong recalled her; the novel places that retreat at the Jidu Nunnery.

ch02.anchor: the high blood of the Ashina house
ch02.note: The Ashina (阿史那) were the royal clan of the Türk khaganates, the line from which every khagan sprang. Türk origin-legend held the house descended from a she-wolf—the source of the wolf-banners, the wolf-headed standards, and the novel’s name for the khagan’s elite, the ‘Wolf Guards.’ For a prince of this house to be hiding inside Chang’an is, as the text says, enough to shake the court.

ch03.note: The sabao (萨宝; from a Sogdian/Middle Persian title for a caravan leader) was a real Tang office: the government-recognized headman of a resident foreign—chiefly Sogdian—community, who also had charge of its Zoroastrian temples and priests. The Sabao Office (萨宝府) administered such communities under loose imperial oversight, which is why the novel’s Great Sabao can both speak for the believers and be leaned on by the court. Corroborated: the office is attested in Tang institutional sources and in the epitaphs of Sogdian sabao in China.

ch03.anchor: Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup
ch03.note: The ‘Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup’ (饮中八仙) are eight celebrated Tang drinkers immortalized in Du Fu’s poem Song of the Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup: He Zhizhang, Li Bai, Li Shizhi, Li Jin (Prince of Ruyang), Cui Zongzhi, Su Jin, Zhang Xu, and Jiao Sui—of whom Jiao Sui alone held no office. Du Fu’s poem opens with He Zhizhang, so the novel’s placing him ‘at their head’ follows the poem. Corroborated: the roster is Du Fu’s; all eight are historical figures of Xuanzong’s reign.

The Pingkang li (平康里), a ward in the northeast of Chang’an close to the imperial city and the examination offices, was the capital’s famous pleasure district, where the registered courtesans lived. It was divided into three lanes (曲); the northern lane—here called the First Lane—was the humblest, frequented by commoners and struggling examination candidates. Corroborated: described in Sun Qi’s late-Tang Beili zhi (北里志, ‘Record of the Northern Ward’).

‘Kunlun slave’ (昆倬奴) was the Tang term for dark-skinned servants brought from the southern seas and beyond; they are stock figures of Tang tales, most famously in the chuanqi story The Kunlun Slave. Old Ge is later specified as a sengqi slave (僵祁奴), that is a Zanj—from the Arabic name for the East African coast—such enslaved Africans reaching Tang China by way of Arab and Persian traders. Corroborated: both terms are attested in Tang sources; see E. H. Schafer, The Golden Peaches of Samarkand.

Li Linfu (李林甫, d. 752) was Xuanzong’s chief minister for nearly twenty years, the archetype of the crafty official—the idiom kou mi fu jian (口蜜腹剑), ‘honey in the mouth, a dagger in the belly,’ was coined for him. His long dominance and his enmity toward the heir apparent form the novel’s political backdrop; here his mansion, once the residence of Duke Li of Wei, adjoins the courtesans’ quarter.

ch03.anchor: the reigning heir apparent, Li Heng
ch03.note: Li Heng (李亨, 711–762), Xuanzong’s third son and heir apparent, is the ‘one person’ the Jing’an Bureau exists to serve. In 756, amid the An Lushan rebellion, he would take the throne as Emperor Suzong. As heir he lived under his father’s ceaseless suspicion—which is why, as the text stresses, the defense of Chang’an is as much a test of him as a charge laid upon him.

ch03.anchor: the calamity of the three commoner-princes
ch03.note: In 737, worked on by Li Linfu and the favourite Consort Wu, Xuanzong deposed his heir apparent Li Ying and, with two other sons, reduced all three to commoners and forced them to their deaths—the ‘calamity of the three commoner-princes’ (三庶之祸). It is the shadow over Li Heng, who inherited the perilous position the dead prince had held.

Sanle cordial (三勒浆) was a Tang drink of Persian origin, brewed from ‘three le’—three myrobalan fruits (haritaki, bibhitaki, and amla) prized in Persian and Indian medicine. It was a fashionable holiday tipple.

ch03.anchor: good thoughts, good words, good deeds
ch03.note: ‘Good thoughts, good words, good deeds’ (Avestan humata, hukhta, huvarshta) is the ethical core of Zoroastrianism—the ‘three goods’ set against the ‘three evils’ of ill thought, word, and deed. That a Tang grandee can quote it is what wins the Great Sabao: the Persian prelate has found at last an official who knows his faith.

ch04.note: Xun Yue (148–209) was a Later Han historian and political thinker; his Shenjian (申鉴, ‘Extended Reflections’), presented to Emperor Xian, is a treatise of statecraft. The maxim Li Bi quotes—fang wei shang, jiu ci zhi (防为上，救次之), ‘prevention comes first, remedy second’—is genuinely from it. Corroborated: the line stands in the received Shenjian.

ch04.anchor: the burning house of the Buddhist scriptures
ch04.note: An allusion to the Parable of the Burning House in the Lotus Sutra: children play on heedless inside a blazing mansion until their father lures them out with the promise of splendid carts. In Buddhist usage the ‘burning house’ (huozhai, 火宅) is the whole world of suffering, from which the Buddha draws sentient beings; the image turns the pavilion’s literal fire into a figure for that peril.

The Five Kennels (wu fang, 五坊) were the five palace establishments that kept the emperor’s hunting birds and hounds: eagles, gyrfalcons, hawks, sparrowhawks, and dogs. A real Tang institution; their keepers, the ‘Five Kennels boys’ (wufang xiao’er), grew notorious in the ninth century for extorting the people under cover of requisitioning feed for the birds. Corroborated: attested in the Tang histories and satirized in Bai Juyi’s New Music Bureau poems.

ch04.anchor: dancing the Sogdian whirl in fetters
ch04.note: The Sogdian Whirl (huxuan wu, 胡旋舞) was a fast Central Asian spinning-dance, hugely popular in Tang Chang’an—the dancer, often a Sogdian girl, turning so rapidly on a small round rug that the eye could scarcely follow. To ‘dance the Sogdian whirl in fetters’ is to be driven into frantic motion while shackled: Li Bi’s image for acting under crippling constraint.

These ‘kingfisher’ ornaments (翠钿, cuidian) were made by the Tang luxury craft of diancui—iridescent blue kingfisher feathers inlaid into gilt-silver settings. Costly and worn by women of rank, they mark Wang Yunxiu out at once as no commoner, which is how Zhang Xiaojing reads the Türks’ mix-up of the two captives.

‘Golden-wound powder’ (jinchuang yao, 金疮药) was the standard Tang battlefield styptic—a powdered herbal medicine dusted on cuts to stop bleeding and stave off festering. ‘Golden’ here is jin, ‘metal’: a golden wound is one made by a blade.

ch05.note: Li Lin (李琳, d. 757), Prince Yong, was a son of Emperor Xuanzong. History remembers him not for polo but for his end: after the An Lushan rebellion he was given a great command in the southeast, and in 757 raised troops along the Yangtze in what the court branded a revolt; he was defeated and killed. The poet Li Bai, who had joined his staff, was arrested and exiled for the association. Corroborated: biographies in the Old Book of Tang and New Book of Tang. The novel’s petty, queasy prince is thus a real historical figure seen years before his ruin.

A quiet stroke of dramatic irony. Yuan Zai (元载, d. 777) is here a forgettable eighth-rank Evaluator whose very name Prince Yong can barely recall—yet history made him the husband of Wang Yunxiu, the same Wang Zhongsi’s daughter whose abduction drives this day’s events, and then a chief minister under Emperor Daizong, one of the most notoriously corrupt of the dynasty, executed for his greed in 777. Corroborated: the marriage and career are recorded in the Tang histories; the poem-exchange of Yuan Zai and Wang Yunxiu was long famous.

Polo (jiju) was a ruling passion of the Tang court, and its grounds were watered—or, for the rich, oiled—to lay the dust, whence this field’s name. It is a historical site: Yang Shenjiao (杨慎交), husband of Princess Changning, a daughter of Emperor Zhongzong, was recorded as sprinkling his polo ground with oil, a byword for their household’s extravagance. Corroborated: the anecdote stands in the New Book of Tang and the Zizhi Tongjian.

The Daming Palace (大明宫), in the northeast of Chang’an, was the vast main palace-complex of the Tang court, its great audience halls the seat of government. Nearby stood the Xingqing Palace (兴庆宫), Emperor Xuanzong’s favoured residence. The two loom over the modest official houses of this ward, as the text explains, because the emperor on the wall could see whose home was plain and whose extravagant.

Silla (新罗) was the kingdom then ruling most of the Korean peninsula. Silla maidservants (Xinluo bi, 新罗婢), like Kunlun (African) pages, were a prized luxury import in the households of the Tang elite—their presence here marks Prince Yong’s rank and wealth.

The bingfang (病坊), also called beitian (悲田, ‘field of compassion’) houses, were Tang charitable infirmaries—originally Buddhist temple foundations, later brought under state supervision—that sheltered and treated the sick and destitute. Cao Poyan’s bafflement that Great Tang would feed such ‘useless mouths’ marks the gulf between steppe and city.

ch06.note: The novel’s shizhi (石脂, literally ‘stone-grease’) is petroleum—the naphtha that seeps to the surface in the northwest. The detail that Yanzhou (modern Yan’an) petroleum was burned for its soot to make a prized ink is genuine history: the Song polymath Shen Kuo, who coined the very word shiyou (石油, ‘rock-oil,’ still the modern Chinese for petroleum), records in his Dream Pool Essays that he made ink from Yan’an petroleum-soot and judged it finer than pine-soot ink. Corroborated.

Menghuo (狩火, ‘fierce-fire’) and its bomb the menghuo lei are the novel’s version of the naphtha incendiary that real Tang and Song armies called menghuoyou (狩火油, ‘fierce-fire oil’)—the distilled-petroleum weapon that reached China from the eastern Mediterranean, kin to Byzantine ‘Greek fire.’ Its use, and purpose-built pump-projectors for it, are described in the Song military compendium Wujing Zongyao (1044). The clinging, unquenchable flame Zhang Xiaojing describes is just what the sources report. Corroborated—though the sealed bursting-jar ‘thunder’ is the author’s own extrapolation.

Jiajie (假节, literally ‘to be lent the tally’) was a real institution of the Han and the Wei-Jin period: the emperor delegated a portion of his own authority to a general or governor by conferring a tally (jie, 节), which carried defined powers of command and of summary punishment. The novel borrows the ancient term for the Jing’an Bureau’s device of routing every watchtower’s reports to a single field commander—a fictional usage, but the text’s gloss of the words (jia = to lend, jie = authority) is faithful to the historical term.

ch06.anchor: the great and towering Wild Goose Pagoda
ch06.note: The Great Wild Goose Pagoda (Dayan ta, 大雁塔), in the grounds of the Ci’en Temple, was raised in 652 to house the scriptures the monk Xuanzang brought back from India. Newly passed jinshi graduates traditionally climbed it to inscribe their names; Zhang Xiaojing’s memory of viewing Chang’an’s peonies from its top belongs to the ordinary city he loves.

ch06.anchor: the Lady Gongsun of the old days
ch06.note: Lady Gongsun (公孙大娘, fl. early 8th c.) was the most celebrated sword-dancer of the Tang. Du Fu, who saw her perform as a child, wrote a famous poem recalling it, and the ‘cursive sage’ Zhang Xu (one of the wine-immortals of Chapter Three) was said to have drawn his wild running-script from the swing of her dancing.

‘Fire-washed cloth’ (huohuanbu, 火浣布) is asbestos, woven into an incombustible fabric that Chinese sources describe being cleaned by casting it into flame. A rare western import, it here forms the ward fire-fighters’ protective cloaks—and, shortly, Zhang Xiaojing’s.

ch06.anchor: the Tang Rhymes compiled by Sun Mian
ch06.note: The Tang Yun (唐韵, ‘Tang Rhymes’) was the standard Tang rhyme-dictionary, revised by the scholar Sun Mian around 751. The watchtowers’ ‘rhyme code’ turns it into a cipher: a character is signalled by its address in the book—scroll, rhyme-group, and number—so that any word can be sent by flag or drum. The semaphore is the novel’s invention, built on a real dictionary.

ch06.anchor: the Sixteen Guards of the Southern Command
ch06.note: The ‘Southern Command’ (Nanya, 南衙) was the Tang metropolitan guard system—sixteen guard-armies under the civil government, so named because their offices lay south of the palace—as against the ‘Northern Command’ (Beiya, 北衙) of the emperor’s own palace armies. Which of the two a plotter controlled tended to decide the outcome of a Tang palace coup.

ch07.anchor: hide away the bow and boil the hound
ch07.note: An allusion to a proverb of statecraft, niao jin gong cang, tu si gou peng (鸟尽弓藏，兔死狗烹)—’the birds all shot, the bow is put away; the hares all caught, the hound is boiled.’ It is credited to the Yue strategist Fan Li and echoed at the fall of the Han general Han Xin: the servant who has won the victory is discarded, or killed, once his use is spent. The condemned Zhang Xiaojing, freshly betrayed by the very office he saved, jokes that his masters have not quite reached that point yet. Corroborated: the saying is recorded in Sima Qian’s Records of the Grand Historian.

Dong Zhongshu (179–104 BCE) was the Confucian scholar whose memorials to Emperor Wu of Han helped make Confucianism the state doctrine. A tomb in Changle Ward was popularly held to be his, and riders dismounted before it in respect, whence its name the Dismount Barrow (下马陵, Xiama Ling). In the local speech xiama slid into the near-homophone hama (虾螂, ‘toad’), and so the mound became, absurdly, the Toad Barrow (虾螂陵)—a corruption the poet Bai Juyi already used in his Song of the Pipa. The pun cannot survive translation and is footnoted here. Corroborated.

Wu Zixu (d. 484 BCE) was a minister of the state of Wu, celebrated in later legend for the night his hair and beard turned white with anxiety as he tried to slip through the Zhao Pass while fleeing his enemies. To compare Li Bi’s haggard, suddenly aged face to his is to say that a single afternoon has worn on the young man like a lifetime of care. Historical figure, legendary detail; the white-hair story is told in the Wu Yue Chunqiu.

ch07.anchor: This rise was called the Leyou Plateau
ch07.note: The Leyou Plateau (乐游原), a loess height in Chang’an’s southeast, was the city’s favourite spot for looking out over the whole capital—paired with Qujiang Pool as the ‘hills and waters’ one could enjoy without leaving the walls. It is the setting of one of the most quoted quatrains in Chinese, Li Shangyin’s later lament that ‘the setting sun is boundless in its beauty—only, dusk is so near.’

The weimao (帷帽) was a wide-brimmed hat with a hanging veil of gauze that fell to the shoulders, worn by Tang women out of doors to screen the face. The device is central to the plan here: behind the veil, one woman can be exchanged for another.

ch07.anchor: bear the bramble-rod and beg punishment
ch07.note: To ‘bear the bramble-rod and beg punishment’ (fu jing qing zui, 负荆请罪) is a set phrase for an abject, sincere apology. It comes from the Warring States tale of the general Lian Po, who, ashamed of having slighted the minister Lin Xiangru, went to him stripped to the waist with a bundle of thorn-rods on his back, offering himself to be flogged.

ch07.anchor: Mount Hua has ever had but one road
ch07.note: ‘From of old, Mount Hua has had but one road’ (自古华山一条路): the sole path up the sheer western sacred peak admits of no alternative, so the saying means a course from which there is no turning back once begun. It becomes Li Bi’s refrain for the ruthless singleness the day forces on him.

ch08.note: Nestorian Christianity—the Church of the East, which the Tang called Jingjiao (景教, the ‘Luminous Teaching’)—reached Chang’an much as the novel says. The monk Alopen (阿罗本) came from Persia in 635, the ninth year of Zhenguan; Emperor Taizong received him, and within a few years a temple stood in Yining Ward, the mother-house of the faith in China. The whole account—down to the cross-borne-on-a-lotus emblem—is preserved on the ‘Nestorian Stele’ (大秦景教流行中国碑), raised in Chang’an in 781 and dug up there in the seventeenth century. Such temples were officially styled Persian Temples (波斯寺) until 745—the year after this one—when Xuanzong decreed them renamed Daqin Temples (大秦寺) after the faith’s true home in Daqin, the Roman Orient; which is why Yisi’s correction, ‘the Daqin Temple, not the Persian Temple,’ runs a year ahead of the calendar. Corroborated.

Li Bi quotes the Daodejing (chapter 5): tiandi bu ren, yi wanwu wei chugou (天地不仁，以万物为刻狗), ‘Heaven and earth are not benevolent; they treat the myriad things as straw dogs.’ The straw dogs (chugou) were figures plaited for a sacrifice, honored while the rite lasted and then trampled and burned: Heaven, the line means, is impartial to the point of indifference, favoring nothing. Unable to hold the hundreds of thousands of lives in his charge at so cold a remove, Li Bi confesses he cannot cultivate his Daoism up to it.

ch08.anchor: labor with their minds govern others
ch08.note: The Right Shad quotes Mencius (Mengzi, ‘Teng Wen Gong’ I): laoxin zhe zhi ren, laoli zhe zhi yu ren (劳心者治人，劳力者治于人), ‘those who labor with their minds govern others; those who labor with their strength are governed by others.’ In Mencius the maxim explains the division of labor between ruler and ruled; in the Right Shad’s mouth it becomes a slaver’s creed—the Wolf Guards the ‘strength’ he spends, himself the ‘mind’ that pockets the profit.

ch08.anchor: warming green-ant wine over a red clay stove
ch08.note: ‘Green-ant wine’ (lüyi jiu, 绿蚁酒) is newly fermented rice wine, named for the greenish froth of lees that floats on it like ants. The picture here—green-ant wine warmed over a small red-clay stove—is lifted straight from Bai Juyi’s famous quatrain inviting a friend to drink against the coming snow.

ch08.anchor: one of the Three Foreign Religions
ch08.note: The ‘Three Foreign Religions’ (san yijiao, 三夷教) were the three Western faiths tolerated for the resident foreigners of Tang Chang’an: Zoroastrianism (祆), Manichaeism (摩尼—the dualist religion of the prophet Mani), and Nestorian Christianity (景教). All three were proscribed in the great persecution of 845, after which they all but vanished from China.

Mishihe (弥施诃) is the Tang Nestorian transliteration of the Syriac məšīḥā, ‘Messiah’—that is, Jesus Christ. Yisi’s account of the crucifixion and the resurrection on the third day is orthodox Christian doctrine, cast in the Buddhist-tinged vocabulary the Tang Church of the East used to make itself understood.

ch08.anchor: called the Daqin Temple, and not the Persian Temple
ch08.note: Nestorian temples were officially styled ‘Persian temples’ (波斯寺) until 745, when Xuanzong—recognizing that the faith came ultimately from the Roman East—had them renamed ‘Daqin temples’ (大秦寺), Daqin being the Tang name for the Eastern Roman lands. Yisi’s little correction runs a season ahead of the official change, which fell the year after the novel’s setting.

ch08.anchor: the Ordinance to Cherish Written Characters
ch08.note: The reverence for written paper (jingxi zizhi, 敬惜字纸)—the belief that the written character is sacred and must not be defiled or wasted—was a real and lasting Chinese custom: paper bearing writing was burned in dedicated furnaces, never simply discarded. The novel gives it the force of an ordinance, so that Registrar Pang’s privy-paper is itself an offence.

ch09.note: The name Long Bo takes for his band, pifu (蚍蜉), is a word for a large ant. It calls up a famous couplet by the Tang poet-statesman Han Yu (768–824): pifu han dashu, ke xiao bu ziliang (蚍蜉撼大树，可笑不自量)—‘ants that would shake a great tree: laughable, their failure to measure their own strength.’ Long Bo’s boast a breath later, that they have come ‘to give this great tree of the Jing’an Bureau a shake,’ turns the sneer into a battle-name, at once bravado and self-mockery. Corroborated: the lines are from Han Yu’s poem ‘To Zhang Ji’ (调张籍).

The xiezhi (獬豸) is a one-horned beast of Chinese legend, able to tell the crooked from the straight; it was said to gore the guilty party with its horn, and so became the emblem of law and of the censors and judges who upheld it—whose court caps were called xiezhi caps. That Cui Qi’s family carries a jade one, rather than the usual auspicious pixiu (貔貅) or qilin (麒麟), marks them, as the jailer says, for a house of the courts; and his bitter joke—that as a traitor he fears its horn—turns the beast’s justice against himself. Corroborated: the xiezhi is described in Han sources such as Wang Chong’s Lunheng.

‘Cave-running’ (paoku, 跑窟) is the novel’s name for the acrobat’s art of scaling walls and skimming over roofs and eaves—what a later age would call qinggong, ‘light-body skill.’ Yisi trained his in the cave-grottoes and sand-hollows of the Western Regions, a nod to the honeycombed cliff-temples of the Silk Road.

ch09.anchor: hung a blue-and-white mourning bell outside the cart
ch09.note: The ‘mourning bell’ (lisang ling, 离丧铃) was a lead-weighted bell hung on a cart bearing the dying or the dead; its dull, distinctive note warned passers-by to stand clear of the ill luck—which is just what lets the cart pass unhindered through the festival crowd.

ch09.anchor: a scroll of the Dengzhen yinjue
ch09.note: The Dengzhen yinjue (登真隐诀, ‘Concealed Instructions for the Ascent to Perfection’) is a real Shangqing Daoist manual compiled by Tao Hongjing (456–536), on meditation, breath control, and the road to immortality. That Li Bi reaches for it under strain marks the Daoist adept the novel makes of the historical statesman.

ch10.note: Lai Junchen (来俊臣, d. 697) was the most notorious of the ‘cruel officials’ (酷吏) who served Empress Wu Zetian: a torturer and judicial murderer whose manual of framing, the Luozhi jing (罗织经, the ‘Classic of Entrapment’), became a byword for the fabrication of cases. He sent countless victims to their deaths before being executed himself in 697, his fall greeted with public rejoicing. Zhou Xing and Zhou Lizhen, named just above, were cruel officials of the same age. Corroborated: see the ‘Biographies of the Cruel Officials’ in the Old Book of Tang.

Ji Wen (吉温, d. 755) was a Tang official infamous as a hatchet-man and extractor of confessions under torture, a client first of the chief minister Li Linfu and later of the general An Lushan; he rose through the Censorate by fabricating cases and was in the end broken in the factional struggles and driven to his death. His installation here to seize the Jing’an Bureau for the Secretariat marks the Right Minister Li Linfu’s move against the heir apparent’s men. Corroborated: see the Old Book of Tang and the Zizhi tongjian.

A shouzhuo (守捉) was a genuine Tang frontier institution: a garrison-post on the borders, smaller than an ‘army’ (军) and larger than a single beacon-fort, manned by settled border troops. The Shouzhuolang—a guild of mercenaries recruited out of these remote garrison-towns, hiring themselves to local governments, military commissioners, and great merchants—is the novel’s own extrapolation from that institution rather than an attested historical body; the chapter glosses the term as it introduces it.

ch10.anchor: the resident-agent courtyards of the ten military commissioners
ch10.note: By Xuanzong’s late reign the Tang frontier was held by ten great regional commands under military commissioners (jiedushi, 节度使)—Fanyang, Hexi, Pinglu, Shuofang, and the rest—each with its own standing army and, in the capital, a ‘resident-agent courtyard’ (liuhou yuan, 留后院) that doubled as its intelligence post. This piling-up of troops on the borders is what let An Lushan, commissioner of three commands at once, rise to overturn the dynasty in 755 (see Chapter Sixteen).

ch10.anchor: The lantern-floats were not lanterns at all
ch10.note: The ‘lantern-floats’ (badeng, 拔灯) were not lanterns but troupes of singers and dancers on great carts, sent up to the capital by the regional governments to grace the Lantern Festival. They paraded the streets after dark and gathered at last before the Xingqing Palace, where the emperor honoured the finest troupe—the ‘Lantern-Crown Red Tally’—by having it help him light the greatest lantern-tower of all.

ch10.anchor: the one Zhou Xing used on Hao Xiangxian
ch10.note: Zhou Xing (周兴, d. 691) was, with Lai Junchen, the most dreaded of Wu Zetian’s ‘cruel officials.’ From him comes the proverb qing jun ru weng (请君入瓮), ‘please step into the jar’: himself accused of treason, Zhou Xing was tricked by Lai Junchen, who asked over dinner how to make a stubborn suspect confess and, on Zhou’s advice—roast him in a great jar—had that very jar heated for Zhou Xing. It is the ‘inviting the guest into the jar’ of the Bureau’s opening trap.

ch11.note: The self-raining pavilion (ziyu ting, 自雨亭) was a genuine luxury of the Tang rich: water was raised to the roof and let fall from the eaves in a curtain to cool the air in the summer heat. The Tang yulin records that the official Wang Hong (王鉷) built such a pavilion at his mansion, its eaves ‘pouring water down on every side,’ and the palace itself had a water-cooled ‘cool hall’ (凉殿) on the same principle. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: A Moonlit Night on the Spring River
ch11.note: ‘A Moonlit Night on the Spring River’ (Chunjiang huayue ye, 春江花月夜) is a celebrated poem by the early-Tang poet Zhang Ruoxu (张若虚, c. 660–720), so admired that later critics called it ‘a single piece that outshines the whole of the Tang.’ The line the newcomer gives—‘a wisp of white cloud drifts slowly off’ (白云一片去悠悠)—is indeed its seventeenth line; the Shouzhuolang use lines of the poem as call-and-response, the doorkeeper’s challenge ‘Spring River’ being its opening words. Corroborated.

Storax (suhe xiang, 苏合香) was an aromatic resin imported into Tang China from the west—held to come from Daqin, the Roman Orient—and prized for perfumes, incense, and medicine. Here it is the cloying scent of the perfumed carriages; that the disguised killer reeks of it, yet carries none of the bookshop’s camphor, is the flaw Tanqi catches. Corroborated: see E. H. Schafer, The Golden Peaches of Samarkand.

The ‘golden peaches’ (jintao, 金桃) were a fabled fruit sent in tribute to the Tang court from Samarkand (Kang); their rarity made them a byword for exotic luxury. A celebrated modern study of Tang foreign imports, Edward Schafer’s The Golden Peaches of Samarkand, takes its title from them.

The sal tree (suoluo, 娑罗; Shorea robusta) is native to India—Tianzhu (天竺), the Tang name for the subcontinent—and sacred in Buddhism as the tree beneath which the Buddha entered nirvana. To have living specimens freighted north and swaddled against the Chang’an cold is a display of fabulous wealth.

The wan emblem (卍) is an ancient Indian and Buddhist auspicious sign, read as ‘myriad’ or ‘ten thousand’—good fortune without end—and a common decorative fret in Tang art. It bears no relation to its twentieth-century Western misappropriation.

ch12.note: Guan Zhong (d. 645 BCE), the statesman who made Duke Huan of Qi the first hegemon of the Spring and Autumn era, is traditionally revered as the patron of the courtesan trade: he is said to have set up the first state-licensed brothels (女闾) in the Qi capital to raise revenue, so a shrine to him in the pleasure quarter is fitting. The detail is a wry historical joke rather than the source’s invention.

ch12.anchor: I, Yuchang, will surely have your life
ch12.note: Yuchang (鱼肠, ‘fish-gut’) is the name of a celebrated dagger of antiquity, short enough to be hidden inside a fish. With it the retainer Zhuan Zhu assassinated King Liao of Wu in 515 BCE, drawing it from a roast fish served at a banquet—the story is told in the Zuozhuan and in the ‘Biographies of Assassins’ of the Shiji. The killer has taken the weapon’s name as his own.

ch12.anchor: The late king Peroz led his whole clan
ch12.note: Peroz III (卑路斯), son of Yazdegerd III, the last Sasanian king of Persia. After the Arab conquest overran the empire he fled east and sought refuge at the Tang court, which gave him an honorary generalship in the imperial guards and, around 661, set up a short-lived nominal Persian Area Command (波斯都督府) in his name; his line then dwindled among the oasis cities of the Western Regions. The episode is historical, recorded in the Old Book of Tang; Yisi’s claim of royal Sasanian descent rests on it.

ch12.anchor: green-vitriol oil, a stuff of the Daoists’ alchemy
ch12.note: ‘Oil of green vitriol’ (lüfan you, 绿矾油) is sulfuric acid, which Chinese Daoist alchemists learned to distil from green vitriol (ferrous sulfate) long before it was known in the West. Here the assassin carries it as a concealed weapon—real Tang alchemical knowledge turned to grim use.

ch12.anchor: This was what Lao Dan meant
ch12.note: Lao Dan is Laozi, the reputed author of the Daodejing. Yuan Zai quotes its chapter 36: ‘what you would shrink, you must first stretch; what you would take, you must first give.’ It is the classic statement of winning by yielding, which he coldly turns into a strategy of seduction.

ch12.anchor: that Land of Bliss to which the good may go
ch12.note: The ‘Land of Bliss’ (Jile shijie, 极乐世界; Sanskrit Sukhāvatī) is the Western Pure Land of the Buddha Amitābha, where the faithful hope to be reborn free of all suffering—the paradise of Pure Land Buddhism, the most widespread devotion of Tang China.

ch13.note: Ksitigarbha (Chinese Dizang, 地藏) is one of the four great bodhisattvas of East Asian Buddhism, the savior who labors among the dead and the damned. His is the mighty vow the text paraphrases: ‘So long as the hells are not empty, I swear I will not become a Buddha; only when all beings are delivered will I myself attain enlightenment.’ Zhang Xiaojing sets the vow beside the Nestorian belief that the Luminous Lord came down to redeem the world, and takes from both the same lesson—that one must answer in the flesh for one’s own choices. Corroborated: the vow is a fixture of the Ksitigarbha tradition.

Taizhen (太真) was the Daoist name of Yang Yuhuan (719–756), the future Yang Guifei (‘Precious Consort Yang’), the most famous beauty of the age. She had first been the wife of Xuanzong’s son the Prince of Shou; to take her into his own harem the emperor had her ordained a Daoist priestess in 740 under the name Taizhen, and made her Guifei in 745—the year after this one—so that here she moves through the palace still as the Daoist ‘Sister Taizhen.’ Her later ruin is the matter of Bai Juyi’s Song of Everlasting Sorrow: in 756, as the An Lushan rebellion drove the court in flight, the mutinous guards forced her death at the Mawei post-station. That Tanqi should know her by this intimate name, at the very foot of the throne, is a stroke of dramatic irony. Corroborated: Old Book of Tang, New Book of Tang, Zizhi tongjian.

The Nichang yuyi wu (霜裹羽衣舞), ‘the Dance of the Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Robe,’ was the most celebrated dance-and-music suite of Xuanzong’s court, its melody traditionally credited to the emperor himself and its dance made famous by Yang Guifei. That its strains should strike up at the very moment Taizhen lays her hand on Tanqi’s shoulder, and the hour of the Rat begins, is a deliberate authorial chord: the dance is bound in memory to the woman now standing here and to the reign whose ruin she would come to stand for. Corroborated: attested in Tang sources and celebrated in Bai Juyi’s Song of Everlasting Sorrow.

The two towers’ names are freighted with meaning. Hua’e xianghui (花萼相辉), “Blossoms and Calyxes Shine on One Another,” draws on a Book of Songs image in which brothers are as the flower to its calyx, each sustaining the other; Emperor Xuanzong raised the tower to feast and lodge with his own brothers, and it became a public emblem of imperial fraternal affection. Qinzheng wuben (勤政务本), “Diligent in Governance, Devoted to the Root,” proclaims the sovereign’s care for statecraft and for agriculture, the “root” of the realm.

The Yellow Lion Dance (黄狮子舞) descends from the Tang court’s Five-Directions Lion Dance, in which five lions of the five directional colors danced to Kucha music; the central lion was yellow, the color of the emperor and of the earth at the center of the world. The yellow lion thus stood for the sovereign himself, which is why the novel makes it a dance reserved to the throne and rarely seen. (Corroborated: the Five-Directions Lion Dance is recorded in the Old Book of Tang, “Treatise on Music.”)

ch14.note: Chao Heng (c. 698–770) is the Chinese name of Abe no Nakamaro (阿倍仲麻吕), a Japanese student-envoy who came to Chang’an with an embassy to the Tang, passed the imperial examinations, and rose to high office under Xuanzong, never managing to return home. A friend of the poets Li Bai and Wang Wei, he was once reported drowned at sea, and Li Bai wrote a famous elegy for him before word came that he had in fact survived. Historical.

The Tianshu (天枢, ‘Axis of Heaven’) was a great commemorative column of bronze and iron raised in 695 before the Duanmen Gate of Luoyang, at the urging of Wu Sansi and the chieftains of the foreign tribes, to glorify Empress Wu Zetian’s Zhou dynasty. Roughly a hundred chi tall, it was pulled down and melted for its metal under Xuanzong some thirty years later. Historical; recorded in the Zizhi Tongjian.

Xu Hezi (许合子, also written 许和子), known as Yongxin (永新) after her home county in Jiangxi, was the most celebrated woman singer of Xuanzong’s court, famed — exactly as here — for a voice that could ring out clear over the din of a vast festival crowd. Her story is preserved in the late-Tang miscellany Yuefu zalu. Historical.

ch15.note: Xiao Gui’s tale deliberately echoes Bai Juyi’s famous ballad ‘The Old Charcoal-Seller’ (卖炭翁, c. 809), a protest against the gongshi or ‘palace-purchase’ system, under which imperial agents seized goods at nominal prices. Bai’s old man burns charcoal in the Southern Mountains (南山) and has a whole cartload — ‘a thousand catties and more’ (千余斤) — carried off by palace buyers for ‘half a bolt of red gauze and a length of damask’ (半匹红纱一丈绫); Ma Boyong borrows the details almost word for word. Bai Juyi (772–846) was among the most widely read of the Tang poets.

ch15.anchor: pinning on a sprig of dogwood
ch15.note: To wear zhuyu (茱萸, dogwood or cornel) was a custom of the Double Ninth festival (重阳), when sprigs were worn to ward off harm — the custom behind Wang Wei’s well-known line, ‘far off I know that where my brothers climb the height, one man is missing as they pin on the dogwood.’ The armies of the Western Regions turned the phrase around: because the ripe dogwood berry is a purplish blood-red, ‘to pin on the dogwood’ became a byword for drawing blood, as the text goes on to explain.

A toumingzhuang (投名状), literally a ‘submitted-name warrant.’ The term comes from the novel Shuihu zhuan (Water Margin): a man seeking to join the outlaws of Liangshan Marsh had first to go out, kill a stranger, and bring back proof of the deed, so that, now guilty of a capital crime himself, he could never return to lawful life. Here Xiao Gui demands the head of Li Bi as the price of Zhang Xiaojing’s good faith.

ch16.anchor: Chen Xuanli, Grand General of the Longwu Army
ch16.note: Chen Xuanli (陈玄礼) was the historical commander of Xuanzong’s palace guard, and the novel places him correctly at the head of the Longwu Army. History remembers him above all for the day the reign this book depicts came to ruin: in 756, as the An Lushan rebellion drove the court in flight to Shu, it was Chen Xuanli’s mutinous guards who at the Mawei post-station forced the emperor to put to death the chief minister Yang Guozhong and the Precious Consort Yang Guifei — the Taizhen who moves through these pages. Corroborated: Old Book of Tang, New Book of Tang, Zizhi tongjian.

A stroke of grim dramatic irony. An Lushan (安禄山, c. 703–757), of Sogdian and Turkic blood, was in 744 only the military commissioner of Pinglu on the northeastern frontier; the guard here, an old trooper of his, remembers him warmly as ‘a good man, a man of honor.’ Eleven years later this same An Lushan raised the rebellion that broke the High Tang, seized both capitals, and drove Xuanzong from Chang’an — the catastrophe whose long shadow the whole novel is written under. Corroborated: Old Book of Tang, Zizhi tongjian; see E. G. Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan.

ch16.anchor: Duke Li of Wei and Jieli Khagan
ch16.note: The tableau of the ‘Wuwei’ lantern-chamber commemorates a real victory: in 630 the Tang general Li Jing (李靖), later ennobled Duke of Wei, made a lightning night march through the Yin Mountains and shattered the Eastern Turkic Khaganate, capturing its ruler Illig Qaghan — the Jieli Khagan (鮕利可汗) of the Chinese sources. The campaign ended the first Turkic empire and won Taizong the title ‘Heavenly Qaghan’ from the northern peoples. Corroborated: Old Book of Tang, Zizhi tongjian, juan 193.

ch17.note: Kuafu (夹父) is a giant of Chinese myth who set himself to race the sun; parched in the chase, he drank the Yellow River and the Wei dry and still died of thirst, and the staff he cast down as he fell grew into a forest of peach trees. The tale is told in the Classic of Mountains and Seas (山海经). Here his colossal, doomed silhouette lends the still-dark lantern-tower its air of menace.

An allusion to Tang (汤), founder of the Shang dynasty. Coming upon a fowler who had spread nets on all four sides and prayed every creature into them, Tang had three sides taken down and bade the beasts go free save those that willed to enter — a proverbial emblem of a ruler’s clemency, and here of the “benevolence” (仁德) the tableau names. The story is recorded in Sima Qian’s Records of the Grand Historian (史记), where Tang opens three sides of the net; the saying later hardened into the common form “open one side,” which the novel follows. Corroborated.

ch17.anchor: the Longchi within the Xingqing Palace
ch17.note: The Longchi (龙池, “Dragon Pool”) lay at the heart of the Xingqing Palace. By tradition a spring welled up on the grounds of Li Longji’s residence while he was still a prince, forming a pool over which a dragon was said to have appeared — read as a portent of his throne; on becoming Emperor Xuanzong he raised the palace around it. The waterway plot turns on the pool being the one point where the conspirators’ flooded tunnel opens into the palace precincts. Corroborated.

ch18.note: The Xuanwu Gate Incident of 626 (the ninth year of Wude): Li Shimin, the future Emperor Taizong, ambushed and killed his elder brother the crown prince Li Jiancheng and his younger brother Li Yuanji at the Xuanwu Gate of the palace, then compelled their father, Emperor Gaozu, to yield him the throne. It became the founding trauma of Tang succession politics and the type-case of the ‘kin-slaying’ strain in the Li house to which Li Bi’s fear here alludes. Corroborated by the standard Tang histories and the Zizhi tongjian.

Two coups by which Li Longji (the future Emperor Xuanzong) rose to power. In the Tanglong coup (710) he and his aunt, Princess Taiping, overthrew Empress Wei—the widow of Emperor Zhongzong, said to have poisoned him and seized power—and put her party to death, restoring Li Longji’s father Ruizong to the throne; in the Xiantian coup (713) the now-enthroned Xuanzong destroyed the faction of Princess Taiping, his former ally, and forced her to take her own life. Both turned on first winning over the palace guards—which is why Chen Xuanli, who lived through them, so dreads moving the Longwu Army unbidden. See the Zizhi tongjian.

Here ‘Changle Ward’ renders Changle fang (长乐坊), a ward in the northeastern city near the Xingqing Palace, where the heir apparent’s residence stood within the Ten Kings’ Residence. It is a different ward from the identically romanized Changle Ward (常乐坊) in the southeastern city, through which the carriage has just passed: the two are written with different characters—长 (‘long’) and 常 (‘ever’)—but fall together in modern pinyin. Li Bi’s alarm turns on the distinction—driving south, away from 长乐坊, the heir apparent is heading the opposite way from home.

ch19.note: The yichun jian (移春欃, ‘spring-moving frame’), a real Tang court conceit: large mobile planter-carts of earth and growing flowers that could be wheeled wherever a movable garden was wanted. They are recorded in the eighth-century miscellany Kaiyuan Tianbao Yishi as a device of Emperor Xuanzong’s pleasure-grounds; the novel turns them into the improvised scaffolding by which the guards reach the broken stair.

ch19.anchor: To govern by virtue is to be as the pole-star
ch19.note: Confucius, Analects 2.1: ‘为政以德，譬如北辰，居其所而众星共之’—he who governs by virtue is like the pole-star, which keeps its place while all the other stars turn about it. The line is quoted to gloss the north-facing imperial seat of the Star-Plucking Hall, the ruler seated motionless at the still point about which the court is ranged.

ch19.anchor: one who holds a hostage is to be struck along with the hostage
ch19.note: A real provision of Tang law: under the Tang Code (捕质, the article on hostage-taking), soldiers were to strike down a hostage-taker without staying their hand for the captive’s sake, the captor being ‘struck together with’ the person he holds. The rule was meant to remove any incentive to seize hostages—but, as the text notes, it is void where the hostage is the Son of Heaven himself. Chen Xuanli invokes it a moment later with the cry ‘Strike the hostage-taker, and do not waver!’

ch20.anchor: Those who eat meat are of mean discernment
ch20.note: Xiao Gui quotes the commoner strategist Cao Gui (曹刿), from the Zuozhuan under Duke Zhuang’s tenth year: when his fellow-villagers asked why he should meddle in a matter the great men were handling, he answered, ‘Those who eat meat are of mean discernment, and cannot lay far-sighted plans.’ ‘Those who eat meat’ (肉食者) meant the ruling class, whose rank entitled them to meat at table; Cao Gui went on to win the Battle of Changshao (684 BCE) for the small state of Lu against the larger army of Qi. Corroborated.

ch20.anchor: When the sovereign is troubled, the minister toils
ch20.note: The line an official shouts—君忧臣劳，君辱臣死, ‘when the sovereign is troubled, the minister toils; when the sovereign is shamed, the minister dies’—is from the Discourses of Yue in the Guoyu, spoken by Fan Li (范蠡) as he took his leave of King Goujian of Yue; it is echoed in the Records of the Grand Historian. It became the classic maxim of a minister’s duty to die for his lord’s honor. Corroborated.

The chiwen (鸱吻, also 鸱尾)—a dragon-headed, fish-tailed ornament set at each end of a hall’s main roof-ridge—was a fixture of Tang palace architecture. The creature was taken for a water-spirit able to call down rain, and so was set on the ridge as a charm to quell fire (魇火), exactly as the text explains. Corroborated.

ch21.anchor: on earth, two branches twined into one
ch21.note: These two lines—zai tian yuan zuo biyi niao, zai di yuan wei lianli zhi—are the most famous couplet of 长恨歌 (Chang hen ge, ‘Song of Everlasting Regret’), the long narrative poem by Bai Juyi (772–846) that laments the love of this very emperor, Xuanzong, for Yang Yuhuan. A biyi bird is a creature of legend with but one wing, able to fly only when paired with its mate; lianli branches are boughs of two trees grown together into one. The novel’s conceit—that Xuanzong dreamed the lines from the mouth of ‘a man surnamed Bai’ kneeling before him—is a deliberate anachronism and a wink to the reader: Bai Juyi would not be born for another twenty-eight years, and would compose the poem only around 806.

Yaluoshan (轧荦山) was the childhood name of An Lushan (安禄山), the half-Sogdian frontier general whose rebellion would shatter the Tang eleven years after the night of this story; the name is thought to render a Central Asian word for a deity of light or of war. Ma Boyong’s invention—a war-god idol named Yaluoshan hidden atop the emperor’s own tower, the secret hinge of the whole plot—turns that half-forgotten fact into a grim joke: the instrument of Xuanzong’s undoing already bears the rebel’s name. (An Lushan himself is introduced earlier in the novel.)

ch21.anchor: of a hundred-li journey ninety li is but the halfway mark
ch21.note: The saying—xing bai li zhe ban jiu shi (行百里者半九十), ‘of those who set out to walk a hundred li, ninety li is but the halfway mark’—comes from the 战国策 (Zhanguo ce, ‘Intrigues of the Warring States’). Its point is that the last stretch of any undertaking is the hardest, so that one is only truly halfway when nine parts in ten are done; the end is where failures fall. That Xiao Gui, a single step from success, should call it to mind is the author’s quiet foreshadowing.

ch22.anchor: Tongwan City that Helian Bobo had raised in his day
ch22.note: Helian Bobo (赫连勃勃, r. 407–425), a Xiongnu chieftain, founded the short-lived Xia kingdom of the Sixteen Kingdoms era and from 413 built his capital, Tongwan (统万城, ‘uniting the myriad realms’), on the Ordos steppe. Its rammed-earth walls were made legendarily hard: the histories record that his overseer tested each finished stretch by driving an awl into it, and where the point sank in so much as an inch the workmen were put to death and their bodies tamped into the wall. The pale ruins still stand in northern Shaanxi.

ch22.anchor: roadside shrine of the god of journeys
ch22.note: The rite of zu (祖) was an ancient sacrifice to the god of roads, offered before setting out on a journey; by extension the word came to mean a farewell feast or send-off. Small shrines to this deity stood along the highways outside a city’s gates, where a traveler—and those seeing him off—would make an offering and bow to pray for a safe road.

ch22.anchor: He who profits most is suspect
ch22.note: ‘He who profits most is suspect’ (利高者疑): the maxim that in any crime or intrigue the party who stands to gain the most is the first to be doubted—the Chinese counterpart of the Roman cui bono (‘to whose benefit?’). It is the hinge on which Li Linfu turns Li Bi’s whole chain of reasoning back upon the heir apparent.

ch23.anchor: a crimson Yinglong flag with a saw-toothed edge
ch23.note: The yinglong (应龙), the ‘responding dragon,’ is a winged dragon of high antiquity in Chinese myth: it is said to have dammed the waters to help Yu the Great drain the great flood, and, earlier still, to have slain the war-god Chiyou for the Yellow Emperor. Here it lends its name and image to the pennant of an imperial express courier. The pennant’s seven saw-teeth stand for the seven days allowed to carry its perishable freight to Chang’an; before it, the text says, even the strictest gate-order counts for nothing.

ch23.anchor: a whole lychee tree must be given up
ch23.note: The novel’s sharpest historical wink. Fresh lychees (lizhi, 荧枝) spoil within days of the picking, yet the Tang court had them rushed north by relay for the pleasure of Yang Yuhuan—the Consort Taizhen of this book (see Chapter Thirteen)—whose fondness for them became the byword for imperial extravagance. Du Mu (803–852) fixed it forever in his quatrain Passing Huaqing Palace: ‘A single horseman in the red dust, and the Precious Consort smiles; / none guesses it is the lychees coming.’ Here the courier rides in the first month, out of all season, the fruit forced in fire-warmed sheds and cut branch and all, run some two thousand li from Fuzhou (in later tradition the source of her lychees) in seven days—an extravagance the gate-commander is careful not to name aloud, only gazing north toward the palace. Corroborated: Du Mu, Fanchuan wenji; New Book of Tang, ‘Biography of Yang the Precious Consort.’

ch23.anchor: a game or two of shuanglu
ch23.note: Shuanglu (双陆, ‘double sixes’) was a race-game for two players, the pieces borne along a board by the throw of dice—a relative of backgammon, thought to have reached China from India by way of the Western Regions. It was a favorite pastime of the Tang, played by monks, palace ladies, and courtiers alike.

ch24.note: These lines are from He Zhizhang’s Yong liu (咏柳, ‘Ode to the Willow,’ also known as the Liuzhi ci, 柳枝词), one of the best-loved short poems of the Tang, known to every schoolchild: Green jade dressed up a tree grown tall, / ten thousand strands hung down in silken cords of green; / who cut out these slender leaves, I cannot say— / the second month’s spring wind is like a pair of shears. That the dying Xiao Gui should quote its willow-and-shears couplet is his coded way of naming the man behind the whole plot: He Zhizhang, the poem’s author and the Director of the Jing’an Bureau (see Chapter Two), whose residence stood in the willow-thick Xuanping Ward on the Leyou Plateau. Corroborated: the poem is He Zhizhang’s, in the standard Tang anthologies.

The Medicine King is the physician Sun Simiao (see Chapter One), in whose former residence the Jing’an Bureau sits. His yinyu wine (茵芋酒) is a genuine prescription of the sort collected in Sun’s Qianjin fang, steeped with yinyu (Skimmia) and other drugs and given for ‘wind’ ailments and paralysis; but yinyu is toxic, and the sources caution against drinking too much at once. The ‘great wind-sickness’ (大风疾, dafeng ji) is the classical name for leprosy and the gravest ‘wind’ disorders. The bitter irony Li Bi leaves unspoken is that the very draught prescribed to treat such sickness, given in excess, is what he used to still He Zhizhang into his unwaking ‘swoon.’

A wengzhong (翁仲) is one of the colossal stone human figures—armored generals and robed officials—set in pairs along the spirit-road before an imperial or noble tomb to keep eternal guard. The name is traditionally traced to Ruan Weng-zhong, a giant general of the First Emperor of Qin whose likeness was cast in bronze; later such tomb-guardian statues took his name. To liken the ash-faced, lifeless Li Bi to a wengzhong is to make of him a graveyard sentinel, drained of all life. Corroborated: the term and its tomb-statuary sense are standard.

ch25.anchor: the Stele of the Propagation in China of the Luminous Religion of Daqin
ch25.note: The famous Nestorian Stele (大秦景教流行中国碑), set up at Chang’an in 781 (the second year of Jianzhong) and inscribed partly in Syriac, records the history of the Church of the East—‘the Luminous Religion,’ Jingjiao—in Tang China; the cleric Yisi is named on it as a patron. Buried during a later persecution of foreign faiths, it was rediscovered near Xi’an around 1625 and stands today in the Stele Forest (Beilin) museum. Corroborated.

ch25.anchor: the tale of Changxin and Zhaoyang
ch25.note: Two Han palaces that stand for the memory of an imperial consort: the Changxin Palace (长信宮), to which the poet Ban Jieyu withdrew when she was supplanted, and the Zhaoyang Hall (昭阳殿) of the favorite Zhao Feiyan. Wang Yunxiu’s dying words—that none could ‘write of Changxin and Zhaoyang’—claim for her a place among such women whose stories outlast them; they are recorded in her Tang biography.

The Deeds of An Lushan (安禄山事迹, An Lushan shiji) is a genuine Tang work in three juan, attributed to one Yao Runeng, of whom nothing else is known. A principal early source on the rebel, its account of the Mawei mutiny does name a ‘Zhang Xiaojing’ (张小敬) as the horseman who shot Yang Guozhong down—a single surviving line that gives the novel both its hero’s name and its premise. Corroborated: the text survives and the notice is real.

ch26.note: Assassin’s Creed is Ubisoft’s open-world video-game series (from 2007), in which a hooded assassin free-runs across a meticulously rebuilt historical city—Jerusalem, Renaissance Florence, and the rest—to carry out killings. The question that seeded this novel was posted on Zhihu (知乎), a Chinese question-and-answer site: where might such a game be set? Ma Boyong’s answer was the Chang’an of the Tang.
